Supervisor's note, Thursday. Sudha, customer support floor.
Two complaints reached me this week, and I nearly handled them the wrong way round.
Ritesh came in calm, as he does most weeks. His story: the night team dumps tickets on him, nobody values him, he is always left out. It is the fifth such story since January. Each has a different villain and the same sufferer.

I checked the logs before responding. Pankaj was right: his hours had been moved. He had been wronged, and he was simply upset about it.

Simran cried in the office corridor today, and my first thought was: here we go again.
I know that's unkind. But in eight months of sitting next to her, every week has had a new villain. The printer technician was out to get her. The manager hates her. The canteen staff did it on purpose. I've started nodding without listening.

I'm Chetan, and for most of last year my phone rang at midnight. It was always Pooja, my oldest friend from college, and it was always someone: the landlord who hated her, the team lead who ruined her life, the cousin who betrayed her. Some of it was surely real. Some of it had been going on since we were nineteen.
One night she said, "You're the only one I have, and even you don't care." I felt the old guilt rise. Then I tried something new. I listened for ten minutes without fixing. Then I asked, "That sounds painful. What do you want to do about it?"
Silence. Then: "I don't know. Maybe talk to HR."
"Good start. And Pooja, I care, but I can't do calls after eleven any more. Sunday lunches, though, I'm always in."
She was cold for a week. Then she came to Sunday lunch and told me what HR said.

Rain had been falling on the Rotterdam tram stop for twenty minutes when Dalia finally said it: she had been accepted for a semester in Lisbon.
Layla's chest went tight. Everyone left eventually. Her dad had. Her best friend at school had. The words came out before she could stop them. "If you go, we're finished. And don't think I'll keep quiet about what you told me about your family."
Dalia's face drained. "You wouldn't."
"Try me."
On the tram, Dalia stared out of the window. At her stop she said, very quietly, "Fine. I'll turn it down."
Layla should have felt relieved. Instead she felt sick. Dalia hadn't chosen her. Dalia was afraid of her. That night Layla lay awake, knowing a yes squeezed out of fear wasn't love, and knowing the first thing she owed Dalia was to take the threat back.

Dear Devika,
I've been thinking about Saturday since I got home. It was lovely to finally meet Kunal when he picked you up. But during our two-hour lunch he texted you five times, asked who each person in your photos was, and said he would prefer you skipped the trek with your college friends. You laughed and said, "He's so protective, na?"
Maybe that's all it is. I don't know him well, and I'm not trying to judge. But when I was your age, someone's protectiveness slowly turned into me asking permission for everything, and I only saw it much later.
So here's the question I wish someone had asked me: do you feel free with him? Free to go on the trek, see your friends, say no without it becoming a big thing?
You don't have to answer me. Just keep asking yourself. And call me any time, about anything.
Love,
Arohi Didi

He said, "I'll call every Sunday at eleven. If you don't pick up, I'll just call again. Bebe and I are always there. Any time."
Jasleen squeezed his hand hard, once, and went inside.

qa.q: How far was Jasleen's in-laws' house?
qa.a: It was only two bus stops past the mandi.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's glance at Gurmeet before answering suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels watched and anxious, checking whether each answer is allowed.

qa.q: Why was Chinmay's promise at the gate a wise choice?
qa.a: Instead of blaming or pushing her to leave, he set a steady Sunday call and said he and Bebe are always there, keeping a safe line open.

qa.q: What might Jasleen's hard squeeze of his hand mean?
qa.a: It may mean gratitude and a silent sign that something is wrong, even though she cannot say it out loud there.

"I've decided," Sumit said quietly to Sachin, his friend since school, at the tea stall outside the gym. "I'm leaving Kavya. Tonight. I'll just tell her and walk out."
Sachin set down his glass. "Tonight? After what you told me about the last time you asked for space?"
"She threw my phone and locked the door. I know."
"Then let's not do this in one jump. Have you talked to anyone who does this for a living?"
"Like who?"
"There are helplines for people in controlling relationships. Men too. They help you plan: where you'd go, what you'd take, who knows."
Sumit rubbed his eyes. "I don't want to make a big thing of it."
"It already is a big thing. Leaving can be the riskiest part. You can stay at my place, but let's call them first, together, from here."
Sumit took out his phone. "Okay. Now, before I lose my nerve."

qa.q: What happened the last time Sumit asked for space?
qa.a: Kavya threw his phone and locked the door.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when he rubbed his eyes?
qa.a: He felt tired and reluctant, not wanting to make a big thing of it even though he was scared.

qa.q: Why was Sachin right to slow down the plan to leave tonight?
qa.a: Because leaving can be the riskiest part, calling a helpline first helps Sumit plan where to go and who knows, with Sachin's place as a backup.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit had walked out that night without a plan?
qa.a: He might face the same anger as before, alone, with no safe place ready and no one who knew, which could put him in more danger.

grounding: A young man about to leave a controlling relationship is helped by a school friend to call a helpline and plan for safety before the big step.

I'm Vikas. Two years ago I could not have written this down, because my partner read everything I wrote.
What I remember most isn't the shouting. It's how small my world had become, and how sure I was that leaving would fix everything in one night. It was Tenzin, my colleague at the library, who stopped me. "Please don't do it alone," Tenzin said. "Call a helpline first. I'll sit with you."
We called from the staff room on a Tuesday afternoon. The counsellor was calm and practical. We made a plan I won't describe here, except to say it had people in it: Tenzin, my aunt in Nagpur, the counsellor, a date.
The day I left was the most frightening day of my life. The counsellor had warned me it might be, and because of that, I wasn't alone for any of it.
Now I tell everyone the same thing: quiet help first, big step second.

qa.q: Where did Vikas and Tenzin make the call?
qa.a: They called from the staff room on a Tuesday afternoon.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel on the day of leaving?
qa.a: Vikas felt more frightened than on any other day, but because the counsellor had warned it might be so and the plan had people in it, Vikas was not alone.

qa.q: Which choice made the frightening day safer for Vikas?
qa.a: Calling the helpline first and making a plan with people in it, Tenzin, the aunt in Nagpur and the counsellor, meant Vikas was never alone on the day of leaving.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Tenzin to say "Please don't do it alone"?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably worried, but chose to offer steady company and a practical first step rather than pressure.
